The research investigates the impact of digital transformation on organization performance in retail industry in Cape Town, South Africa. The research investigates key drivers such as operation efficiency, technology advancement, cybersecurity, omnichannel retailing, customer behavior, and data-driven decision-making, enabling the adoption of digital transformation in the retail industry. The research investigates how digital transformation initiatives such omnichannel, data analytics, e-commerce, Customer Relationship Management systems, artificial intelligence improves operation efficiency, customer experience and gain competitive advantage. The research investigates the impact of digital transformation on financial performance metrics, such as revenue and cost efficiency. The research also investigates how digital transformation influence operation efficiency through collaboration, automation, data-driven decision-making, and supply chain management. The research investigates the gap between the research background and current research to determine future research on digital transformation in the retail industry. The p investigates challenges and barriers such as skill gap, digital literacy, poor infrastructure, employee resistance, cost constraints, limited access, and regulatory compliance, and how it is affecting the adoption of digital transformation in the retail industry in South Africa.

detail.abstract: The Indian Railways, as one of the world's largest public sector employers, plays a critical role in India's economic growth, connectivity, and social integration. Despite its scale, the institution faces persistent challenges in managing its human resources effectively. This paper critically examines the human resource (HR) practices and grievance redressal mechanisms within the Indian Railways, with a focus on employee welfare, working conditions, and systemic inefficiencies. Drawing upon mixed-method research-comprising both primary observations and secondary data-the study reveals that outdated technology, ineffective recruitment processes, and insufficient employee engagement contribute to declining morale and operational inefficiencies. While recent digitization initiatives such as the Human Resource Management System (HRMS) and the NIVARAN grievance portal have improved transparency, significant gaps remain in welfare policies, performance appraisal, and grievance handling. The findings suggest that reforming HR practices and fostering a culture of participative management are essential to enhance employee satisfaction, productivity, and organizational effectiveness in the Indian Railways.

detail.abstract:
Acknowledging that traditional dispute prevention and resolution mechanisms alone cannot provide the tax certainty needed by businesses in an efficient manner, the authors highlight the key role that programmes such as Cooperative Compliance (CC), the International Compliance Assurance Programme (ICAP) of the OECD, the European Trust and Cooperation Approach (ETACA) of the EU Commission and the Finnish Cross-border Dialogue (FCBD) can play for this purpose. This article illustrates the main characteristics of a plethora of national CC programmes around the world as well as of cross-border risk assessment and assurance programmes (ICAP, ETACA and FCBD), it examines their positive aspects and benefits, the challenges that they present and elaborates on relevant legal considerations. Lastly, the authors identify the limits of existing domestic and cross-border risk assessment and assurance programmes, and propose a new approach to help address these limitations: multilateral CC (MCC) programmes that will provide tax certainty in respect of all tax aspects of large cross-border projects (project-related MCC or, simply, PMCC programmes).

title: Moral Licensing at the Top: How CEO Awards Influence Corporate Pollution
affiliations: Maastricht University - School of Business and Economics and University of Adelaide

detail.title: Moral Licensing at the Top: How CEO Awards Influence Corporate Pollution
detail.abstract: Moral self-licensing theory posits that individuals who build a positive moral self-image through past good deeds may feel justified in acting less ethically afterward. This theory has been well-documented among individuals through experimental studies, but its application to complex organizations remains underexplored. This study examines the theory in corporate finance context, using CEO reputation - proxied by prestigious awards - as moral credit and firm pollution as a measure of ethical conduct. We find that firms led by award-winning CEOs have significantly higher pollution of around 14 percent following the award. The effect is amplified when CEOs hold greater equity-based pay, suggesting a financial motive, as our data show that higher pollution is linked to stronger financial firm performance. These findings highlight how reputational capital can foster moral self-licensing, showing that CEO moral credit may weaken corporate sustainability.

title: The Democratization of Peer Leadership through Group Emotional Intelligence in Groups
affiliations: Rhema Univeristy, Nigeria.

detail.title: The Democratization of Peer Leadership through Group Emotional Intelligence in Groups
detail.abstract: This study based on the investigation literature review research design explored the relationship between the democratization of peer leadership through group emotional intelligence in groups. Leadership is both the adhesive that binds a work group together and the catalyst that encourages members towards productive activities. Peer leadership in a group context is crucial to the development of future leader in organizations of all types and sizes, and equipping the individuals for solving problems intelligently through the use of self-insights and emotional intelligence competencies to assess their responses and to make appropriate action plans. The growing use of groups in organizations has created keen interest in determining what makes them effective so that their success can be holistically facilitated. In many organizations or institutions, cross-functional groups are used at different levels to promote better informed, more innovative decisions and quicker response times. It is believed that this process requires an understanding of the important role of emotion and intelligence in groups. This cannot be overstated because many human emotions grow out of special interactions because emotion is a pervasive influence in groups and is fundamentally linked to how group members interact and work together-irrespective of their diverse backgrounds. The ability of the peer leader to intelligently manage emotions in groups results in developing group emotional intelligence necessary for group performance and cohesion. Group emotional intelligence reflects the ability to develop a set of norms to manage emotional processes so as to cultivate trust, motivation, group identify, and group efficiency. An artful combination of the power of global emotional intelligence and its multidimensional competencies helps in motivating group members as well as the democratization of peer leadership in groups as against the idea of democratic dictatorship in groups. Peer leadership and group emotional intelligence, encompass the ability to motivate group members. This motivation typically involves using influence techniques that appeal to logic or emotion to generate enthusiasm for the work, commitment to group objectives and compliance with requests for cooperation , resources, or assistance and setting an example of positive role behavior in groups. Based on the methodology of this work, the result showed significant positive relationship between the democratization of peer leadership through group emotional intelligence in groups. This study was not exhaustive due to lack of relevant current literature in the areas and research funding. Further study should examine the relationship between team failure and management failure in Nigeria as a measure of reducing the consequences of bad organizational leadership. The study recommends that peer leadership must emphasize the idea of democratic participation rather than democratic dictatorship which often imposes the wishes of the leader on a passive majority.

detail.abstract: Research suggests evaluators' numerical performance ratings of employees tend to exhibit leniency, which can significantly diminish the value of performance evaluations. We investigate whether receiving employees' numerical self-ratings of their performance leads evaluators to provide higher performance ratings than they would otherwise and whether this effect is more pronounced among male versus female evaluators. Using an experiment, we find that, consistent with our theoretical predictions, male evaluators provide lower numerical ratings than female evaluators, providing employees' self-ratings to evaluators significantly increases their ratings, and this effect is more pronounced among male than female evaluators. Also, evaluators forming a preliminary rating before receiving an employee's self-rating does not mitigate this effect. By providing insight into how a key component of the evaluation process, employee self-ratings, can interact with evaluator gender to affect leniency, we highlight the potential for the objectivity and usefulness of performance evaluations being comprimised, particularly among male evaluators.

title: CEO Cultural Values and Environmental Performance: The Role of Heritage and Long-Term Orientation
affiliations: Maastricht University - School of Business and Economics, Maastricht University - Department of Finance and Auckland University of Technology - Faculty of Business & Law

detail.title: CEO Cultural Values and Environmental Performance: The Role of Heritage and Long-Term Orientation
detail.abstract: This study examines how CEOs' deeply rooted cultural values shape corporate environmental performance. Based on U.S.-listed firms, we show that higher Long-Term Orientation characterizes CEOs whose cultural heritage is associated with stronger environmental outcomes that reflect credible performance, but not with environmental intentions that are more symbolic or signaling in nature. This contrast highlights how managerial discretion and decision ambiguity amplify the influence of personal values. The association is stronger when the CEO's connection to their cultural heritage is more pronounced, further supporting the idea that cultural values relate to managerial priorities under high discretion. These findings are robust to multiple specifications, including an instrumental variable, an alternative cultural construct, and the use of a different environmental performance measure. This study contributes to the literature by offering new insights into how cultural values shape complex corporate decision-making in a sustainability context, which requires balancing competing objectives.

title: From Moore's Law to Market Rivalry: The Economic Forces That Shape the Semiconductor Manufacturing Industry
affiliations: International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE), International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE), University of California, Berkeley - Business & Public Policy Group and Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)

detail.title: From Moore's Law to Market Rivalry: The Economic Forces That Shape the Semiconductor Manufacturing Industry
detail.abstract: The semiconductor manufacturing industry exhibits unique competitive dynamics driven by Moore’s Law and Rock’s Law, which together impose exponentially increasing technological requirements and capital costs. These twin forces produce recurring “competitions for the market” rather than conventional price-based rivalry, with firms competing through massive preemptive investments in successive technology generations. In this environment, apparent market concentration and complex interfirm relationships likely reflect efficient organizational responses to extreme capital requirements and technological uncertainty. High returns in this industry typically represent Ricardian and Schumpeterian rents from innovation rather than monopoly profits. Standard antitrust metrics may mischaracterize competition in industries where technological discontinuities periodically reset market positions and where success depends on dynamic capabilities rather than static efficiency.

title: Bank-Focused Term Reverse Repos: A Policy Tool for Gradual Liquidity Management, Fiscal Efficiency and Inflationary Pressure Control

detail.title: Bank-Focused Term Reverse Repos: A Policy Tool for Gradual Liquidity Management, Fiscal Efficiency and Inflationary Pressure Control
detail.abstract: This white paper explores the concept of a bank-focused term reverse repurchase (RRP) facility as a monetary policy instrument designed to manage liquidity, control short-term inflationary pressures, and maintain low policy rates. By allowing banks to park excess reserves for a fixed term 30-90 days at a slightly higher-than-IORB rate, the Federal Reserve could drain liquidity, control short-term inflationary pressures, and maintain low policy rates, thereby protecting fiscal costs and avoiding the market disruption associated with sharp interest rate hikes or large-scale asset sales. The approach aims to balance monetary stability with fiscal efficiency by avoiding sharp increases in Treasury borrowing costs. This paper outlines the operational design, macroeconomic and fiscal implications, quantitative analyses of the proposal, and compares it to traditional tools such as the overnight RRP, intereston-reserves (IOR), and yield-curve control (YCC) strategies.

title: Soldiers in Robes: Why Military Lawyers Can Not and Should Not Serve as Immigration Judges
affiliations: Emory University School of Law

detail.title: Soldiers in Robes: Why Military Lawyers Can Not and Should Not Serve as Immigration Judges

publicationDetails.journalName: Emory University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Department of Justice recently appointed 25 temporary immigration judges, two-thirds of whom are military lawyers, or JAGs, to adjudicate civil immigration cases. The Pentagon says it plans to send hundreds more JAGs to help relieve the strain on immigration courts. These unprecedented moves violate federal law and breach a foundational American principle: military power must not be wielded over civilians in domestic affairs.

Immigration judges are typically career civil employees who are appointed by the Attorney General to serve as administrative judges. Assigning JAGs these positions violates the Posse Comitatus Act, a key law that prohibits the military from “executing” civilian laws. Besides being against the law, the appointments are a bad idea. They breach the foundational norm separating military authority from civilian governance. It would be as if active-duty military officers were assigned to serve as tax court judges or administrative law judges, proposals that would immediately raise constitutional concerns.

The plan to reassign hundreds of JAGs also removes them from the military, where they are needed to provide critical legal advice, including on the deployment of the National Guard to U.S. cities and the use of lethal force, including in the Caribbean.  Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to sideline military lawyers (including firing the top uniformed JAGs in February), the counsel provided by JAGs on complex legal matters is more important than ever. Congress, which has the constitutional authority to make rules for the “Government and Regulation of land and naval forces,” should closely scrutinize any effort to hollow out the JAG Corps.

title: The Discourse Spiral Hypothesis Five Self-Reinforcing Mechanisms in Public Deliberation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Discourse Spiral Hypothesis Five Self-Reinforcing Mechanisms in Public Deliberation
detail.abstract: Public deliberation degrades through five reinforcing mechanisms: (R1) perceptual inertia, (R2) critical escalation, (R3) status competition, (R4) purity policing, and (R5) concept creep. These positive-feedback loops interact to produce superlinear increases in discourse intensity even when underlying conditions are stable; digital platforms amplify but do not create these dynamics. We operationalize each spiral with measurable indices and derive eight predictions about interaction, thresholds, compensation, and cultural moderation. The hypothesis is falsified if platform-only interventions eliminate dysfunction without changes in psychological capacities, if controlled offline studies show no spiral dynamics, if analogous patterns are absent in pre-digital corpora, if single-mechanism fixes succeed without compensation, or if the spirals lack cross-cultural generality. We outline empirical tests, measurement protocols, and a dual-track intervention strategy-platform design dampeners plus psychological-capacity training (emotion regulation, inhibitory control, ambivalence tolerance).

title: Towards a EU Impact Investing Framework
affiliations: Universite du Luxembourg - Faculty of Law, Economics and Finance, University of Luxembourg - Faculty of Law, Economics and Finance (FDEF), University of New South Wales (UNSW) - UNSW Law & Justice and The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Towards a EU Impact Investing Framework

declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge the financial support of the Luxembourg National Research Fund (FNR), grant reference NCER22/IS/16570468/NCER-FT, the Hong Kong Research Grants Council Senior Research Fellow Scheme (Digital Finance and Sustainable Development) and the Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship (FL200100007). The views herein are solely the authors and not necessarily the views of these funding bodies.

detail.abstract:
Sustainability-oriented investors want to pay for impact, not compliance. We analyse the regulatory challenges and opportunities of impact investing. We find that advancing impact investing requires a departure from the EU Sustainable Finance Framework's (EUSFF) prevailing input-orientation and an adjustment of EU asset-management law towards an EU Impact Finance Framework. 

In its current form, the EUSFF over-emphasises exclusion, using rule-based ex ante definitions of sustainable business (herein termed input). If a large share of global capital follows these rules, unsustainable firms’ capital costs will increase, furthering innovation of sustainable alternatives. However, the EUSFF alone cannot prevent global capital flows into unsustainable investments, and non-EU countries follow different approaches. Although the EUSFF encourages, in effect, the sale of unsustainable EU businesses to non-EU firms, its input orientation has not helped the planet: the same activities continue elsewhere, often under weaker environmental and social standards, leaving the planet worse off. Further, the EUSFF’s disregard for proven ex post impacts risks large-scale capital misallocation and “impact washing”. Worse, the input focus comes at the cost of investments paired with audited evidence of positive ESG impacts ex post.

We argue for shifting EU financial regulation from input to (proven) impact. Yet, rather than adding a new product category, we propose recognising positive impacts through five fine-tuned steps that simplify EU financial regulation, taking into account regulatory developments in the United Kingdom and Switzerland. These include abolishing the link between “do no significant harm” under the Taxonomy Regulation and the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, simplified reporting aligned with product materials and the emerging IFRS Disclosure Standards, introducing a new proportionality threshold for mid-sized AIFMs, and revising ESMA’s rules on fund names.

title: Acceding to the Refugee Convention: Indonesia's Persistent Reluctance
affiliations: Faculty of Law Universitas Padjadjaran (UNPAD)

detail.title: Acceding to the Refugee Convention: Indonesia's Persistent Reluctance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Participants involved in this research have given either written or oral consent and are cited in this chapter by the name/ pseudonym they wished.
declarations.funderStatement: The research for this chapter was funded by LPDP—Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education Agency.

detail.abstract:
Despite being host to large numbers of refugees, many countries across Asia and the Middle East remain non-signatories to the Refugee Convention. The rationale behind their lack of accession is not completely clear, but scholarly explanations include Eurocentrism in the drafting of the convention, fear of increased social and economic burdens, and differing experiences of refugeehood. However, much of the research on this topic has been based on general observations about the creation of international refugee law, and observational comparisons of dominant region and state narratives. Limited attention has been paid to the internal dynamics of individual states, and the engagement of actors in domestic politics with the international refugee regime.

This paper aims to address this gap by drawing on empirical research into non-accession, taking Indonesia as a case study. The research utilizes document analysis together with interviews with officials from the Indonesian government, UNHCR, and civil society organizations. The paper puts forward three main factors contributing to Indonesia’s reluctance to accede to the instruments of international refugee law. Firstly, accession is not favored due to the narrative of Indonesia as a transit country for refugees seeking sanctuary in a third country. Secondly, the ‘silo mentality’ among  government agencies impedes decision-making to acceding those instruments. Thirdly, an anti-foreign sentiment, linked to Indonesia’s colonial history, pervades.

The paper will nonetheless show how non-accession is not unanimously supported. Various government and civil society actors are found to have played an active role in shaping the discourse on (non)accession to the Refugee Convention. Importantly, the influence of these different actors has led to a gradual adoption and integration of core international refugee law principles into state policy and practice. Overall, the chapter will demonstrate how colonial histories may impact the way independent states relate to international legal instruments, and shed light on how interactions between state, civil society, and international actors have influenced Indonesia’s adoption of refugee law norms.

title: Prospects for Creating Digital Platforms in EAEU
affiliations: Moscow State University of International Relations (MGIMO University)

detail.title: Prospects for Creating Digital Platforms in EAEU
detail.abstract: Currently, much attention is paid to the creation of digital platforms in the EAEU. The foundations of digital interaction between countries were laid in such documents as the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union (2014), the EAEU Digital Agenda until 2025 and the Strategy for the Development of Eurasian Economic Integration until 2025. In 2019, the first joint project "Eurasian Network of Industrial Cooperation, Subcontracting and Technology Transfer" was launched. Among the main areas of development, the main ones are digital industrial cooperation, the creation of digital transport corridors, digital agriculture, digital trade and the Work Without Borders project. The article analyzes the main results of the programs to date and considers the problems and prospects in the implementation of these projects. The creation of digital transport and logistics corridors and platforms in the EAEU is actively developing. Navigation seals are being introduced, a single "showcase" of digital logistics services is being created, and transparency is increasing. It is expected that the transit time due to the implementation of the program will decrease from 15 to 4-9 days, and the share of transit will increase from 2% (for 2021) to 20%. The Roadmap of the EAEU and China in 2023 on the digitalization of transport corridors was signed. Discussions are underway with Iran on the digitalization of railway corridors. Since 2021, the project "Work without Borders" has been operating, but there are also difficulties with its implementation. If the number of resumes on the platform has grown over the past year, the number of vacancies, on the contrary, has decreased. There are difficulties I have with employment in another country, including requirements for language skills and obtaining a visa. The Eurasian Network of Industrial Cooperation, Subcontracting and Technology Transfer project has been operating since 2019, but in 2024 it was decided to restart it to improve efficiency. Thus, the development of digital platforms in the EAEU is a very promising area, but it is necessary to resolve issues related to the low level of funding, the fragmentation of local information systems, and the technological lag.

title: "Impact of Social Media on Online Shopping Behavior Among Generation Z and Millennials: Basis for Shopping Guide Plan"

detail.title: "Impact of Social Media on Online Shopping Behavior Among Generation Z and Millennials: Basis for Shopping Guide Plan"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest. This research study titled “Impact of Social Media on Online Shopping Behavior among Generation Z and Millennials: Basis for Shopping Guide Plan” is an original work and has not been previously published or submitted elsewhere for any degree or academic recognition. The authors confirm that there are no financial, personal, or professional relationships that could be construed as influencing the results or interpretation of this study.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of social media on the online shopping behavior of Generation Z and Millennials in Batangas City, Philippines, as a basis for developing a Shopping Guide Plan. It examines how social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok influence three key dimensions of consumer behavior: product discovery, decision making, and shopping habits. Using a descriptive research design, data were gathered from 150 respondents through face-to-face and online surveys. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, weighted mean, t-test, and one-way ANOVA to determine generational differences. Findings show that most respondents belong to Generation Z (15-25 years old), followed by Millennials (26-30 years old). The majority were female (61.3%) and single (84.7%), with nearly half being students (44.0%) and full-time employees (42.7%). This represents a young, socially active group highly engaged in digital platforms. Results indicate that social media significantly influences product discovery by introducing new products and shaping awareness among consumers. Its impact on decision-making is moderate, as buyers still consider price, quality, and credibility. Regarding shopping habits, social media promotes browsing, saving items for later, and participating in time-limited deals and live selling. Generation Z tends to be more impulsive and trend-driven, while Millennials show a more practical approach. Based on these findings, a Shopping Guide Plan emphasizing affordability, trend-awareness, and digital engagement was developed to encourage informed and responsible online shopping.

title: On Artificial Intelligence and Network Effects
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: On Artificial Intelligence and Network Effects
detail.abstract: Network effects have long been identified as a significant driver of growth for digital platforms. Emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies stands to interact with network effects in significant ways. While several scholars argued that network effects can accelerate the success of AI, it remains less clear how AI-enabled tools themselves might reshape the competitive advantage digital platforms gain from network effects. In this article, I examine the implications of AI tools for network effects. I argue that while some use cases of AI can amplify network effects, others may weaken them. In particular, when the AI tools reduce search and production costs and reduces shared experiences among consumers, AI may reduce the importance of network effects to a digital platform. The paper concludes with the note that new technologies such as AI can have important implications for competition policy and antitrust enforcement.

title: Unveiling the Forces Driving Expert Activity: The Impact of Information Environment and Peer Behavior on Expert Reviewer Engagement Behavior
affiliations: , Harbin Institute of Technology, Kwantlen Polytechnic University and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Unveiling the Forces Driving Expert Activity: The Impact of Information Environment and Peer Behavior on Expert Reviewer Engagement Behavior
detail.abstract: Online platform engagement with customers, especially those with high expertise, is crucial for companies. As these expert customer reviews directly impact a company's brand image and sales volume, an understanding of expert reviewer engagement behavior (EREB) is critical for companies' marketplace success. This study explores the factors that influence EREB from two key situational cues: those from the company's information environment and from peer expert behavior. Data from 144,634 Yelp reviewers and 5,080 restaurants were analyzed. The results reveal that companies with higher aggregate ratings are more likely to encourage EREB. The impact of overall and peer expert rating inconsistency on EREB varies: Overall rating inconsistency has a positive effect, while inconsistency among expert peers has a negative effect. Additionally, EREB exhibits herding and differentiation patterns in response to changes in peer expert engagement density. This results in a U-shaped relationship between EREB and peer expert engagement density, moderated by aggregate rating, overall rating inconsistency, and peer expert rating inconsistency. This study provides practical insights for marketers looking to engage expert customers and expands on the literature on expert customer engagement behavior.

title: Resonance of Review Behavior: Will People Follow in Their Friends' Footsteps?
affiliations: , Harbin Institute of Technology, University of Macau and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Resonance of Review Behavior: Will People Follow in Their Friends' Footsteps?
detail.abstract: This study investigates factors affecting users' review behavior on electronic word-of-mouth platforms, with a focus on the motivating influence of friends' review contributions. Drawing on the theory of competitive altruism, we analyze how users perceive reputation-related competition on a platform. We additionally identify attributes related to friends, users, and companies that influence users' review contributions. We obtained data from Yelp and constructed a dataset of more than two million user-restaurant-week triads for analysis. The findings suggest that amateur friends' reviews more strongly affect a user's likelihood of reviewing than expert friends' reviews. In addition, users who have gained expert status are less influenced by their friends' reviews than amateur users. As users' review experience and social reach increase, the roles of friends' reviews diminish when a person has a lower status than their friends. Moreover, the motivations stay focused on the reviewed company and do not spill over to other companies even when the motivations are recurring and prolonged. Following expert friends leads to user reviews that are more readable. Competing with low-status friends can afford users a reputational advantage particularly when these users have a higher status.
